result.note: Tests the July 2026 amendment bill to the Public Examinations Act 2024: its penalties, timelines and the courts designated for trials.

questions.prompt: Consider the following statements about the bill on public examination malpractices introduced by the Centre in July 2026:
items: It was introduced in the Lok Sabha and proposes amendments to the Public Examinations Act of 2024.
Individual cheaters would face 5–10 years in prison, up from 3–5 years.
Complicit service providers would face a ban from public-examination work of eight years, double the current period.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explain: The story supports all three statements. The bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 27 July 2026, raising prison terms for individuals and doubling the ban on service providers from four to eight years. It follows years of high-profile paper leaks, including the alleged NEET-UG leak.
questions.source: Complicit service providers would face fines of up to INR 5 crore (~USD 518 thousand) and an 8-year ban from public-examination work, double the current four.

questions.prompt: Consider the following pairs relating to the Public Examinations Act amendment bill introduced in July 2026:
items: Maximum fine for individual offenders — INR 50 lakh
Maximum fine for organised offences — INR 5 crore
Deadline for completing investigations — two months
questions.ask: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.explain: Organised offences would carry fines of up to INR 10 crore and at least seven years in prison. INR 5 crore is the maximum fine for complicit service providers. The individual fine ceiling rises fivefold to INR 50 lakh, and investigations must finish within two months.
questions.source: Organised offences would carry at least seven years and fines of up to INR 10 crore (~ USD 1 million).

questions.prompt: Under the bill on public examination malpractices introduced in the Lok Sabha in July 2026, which courts would be designated as Special Fast Track Courts?
questions.explain: The bill designates Courts of Session as Special Fast Track Courts. These courts would hold day-to-day trials with a three-month deadline from charge sheet to verdict. TBB notes that the 2024 law had already made paper leaks non-bailable.
questions.source: with Courts of Session designated as Special Fast Track Courts running day-to-day trials and a three-month deadline from charge sheet to verdict.
